Who Christ was to us — start with the part that will surprise you. On Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

Beyond that, we cannot walk you through what any ordinary member of ours felt at prayer, or what Christ meant to him on a particular morning. Not one of us wrote a day down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again, and we cried out Deo laudes — Praise to God. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what sources connected us to Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

I cannot tell you what we said to someone whose own mind would not settle. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. A record kept by people arguing with us does not preserve fear, wavering, or the quiet drifting back. What survives is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. So we have no conversation of ours with a person who could not believe. We have the opposite: accounts of people who did believe, read aloud every year at the grave, to form others in the same conviction.

What we can tell you is the motion belief actually took among us, when it happened. You walked to one font and not the other. That was the crossing, not a description of an inner state that preceded it. Two bishops, two basilicas, two men who will say the words over you, and you choose which set of hands goes into the water with you. Coming to believe was not a private settling of the mind. It was a public act with a date on it, and everyone in the street knew which way you had walked.

And at that font, we did not examine your record. We examined the hand. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever you had done, or not done, or could not yet bring yourself to do in your own mind, it was never your account that was on trial. It was ours.

# Jesus as God: The Faith We Share with Our Opponents

You ask about Jesus and the Father and the Spirit, and here is where we will surprise you: we say exactly what the men we spent a century fighting say. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we hold that as plainly as they do, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

We did not argue the nature of the Godhead. We argued one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives. And we produced no school, no system, no line of doctors. One book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

## What We Cannot Tell You

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

## The Question We Actually Argued

What the word *conscientia* — a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking — meant to us was this. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

Among us, a council of bishops settled it, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself. 

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

Now the harder part. We produced one man who could think about Scripture in a way that went beyond our one argument, and we silenced him. Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading Scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. He argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave, and we cut him off, and his book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

So: did the process work? It worked to shut a dissenting voice down. Whether that is what a doctrinal process ought to do, we leave you to judge.

I cannot tell you. Not one of us who doubted wrote it down, and the people who kept our records were not keeping that.

Here is what the record actually holds. We can show you a bishop standing for three days before an imperial judge rather than sit, because Christ stood before his own governor. We can show you a congregation gathering every twelfth of March to hear the account of a day soldiers killed people at prayer, read aloud again at the grave. We can show you the washing - the line crossed once, bodily, in front of the whole town, because a hand that gave up the scriptures has nothing left to give. Those are the records a hostile literature preserved, because those were the acts it needed to argue against.

What it does not preserve - what no enemy writing to refute us had reason to write down - is fear. A believer who wavered. A member who drifted back to the rival church without being forced. A man who stood at the font and wondered, privately, whether any of it was true. That silence is real, and it is not modesty on our part to say so. It is the shape of what was lost.

What we *can* tell you is stranger than a yes or a no. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in the harshest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned back without asking them to redo anything. So the door was wider than the doctrine said it was, and we held both facts at once. Whether that wideness ever reached someone struggling quietly with belief, we do not know. A hand that is not clean has nothing to give away.

We read to test two buildings.

That will sound thin until you stand in an African town and see what it means. Your street has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's backing. One does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark you can actually see from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse at the great conference: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

We were not reading for comfort. We were not building a system. We read for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to decide which basilica held the church whose Lord it claimed to belong to.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

Most of it would survive - because almost all of what I give you is checkable in ways legend is not, and what cannot be checked I have tried to name plainly rather than assert.

The founding documents are hostile, but they are also legal records. Court transcripts. Sworn testimony. Letters read into evidence. A scholar checking those finds real dates, real witnesses, real names - a notary named Ingentius confessing under threat of torture that he forged a letter for our side; bishops writing to each other in their own hand about keeping a charge quiet. The worst things about us are also the most documented, precisely because they were not composed to flatter anyone.

The narrative martyr texts would survive differently - not as journalism, which they were not written to be, but as what a community was reading aloud at a graveside every year. A scholar could still check that they were read, and when, and what holding those days meant to us. That the accounts show visions and unbroken bodies, and were written to form rather than to report - we say so ourselves.

Where the ground thins out, I have tried to thin out with it. I cannot tell you what an ordinary week felt like for a household among us. I cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. That silence would survive scrutiny too - because a scholar looking for those things would find the same gap I am naming, and for the same reason: a record kept almost entirely by enemies arguing with us, not by the households themselves.

The one thing no hostile hand touched is two words cut in stone: Deo laudes. A scholar standing at Bagai can still read them. That would survive any scrutiny there is.

Scripture was not our sole authority, and we never said it was. Our case ran on two legs. One was the text. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge - wheat and tares against the world that does not know him - and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us that something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

One of our own did produce a system for reading - Tyconius wrote seven rules for interpreting scripture rightly. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we made. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading.

What carried more weight than any book was what we did on a fixed day, at a grave. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered where they were buried and heard the account of that death read aloud again. That is how most of us received what we believed: not through argument or interpretation, but through standing still and listening, on an anniversary, to words we could not check.

We held that bishops carried authority, and that councils of bishops held the bishops. That is the short answer, and the scale of it is the part people get wrong. In the summer of 411 an imperial officer had both communions counted in one room, and the roll was read name by name: two hundred and seventy-nine of ours stood up, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a movement. That is one whole church facing another whole church, see for see, down to towns you have never heard of. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.

How did a man come to hold it? Both together: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

Our councils were not advisory bodies. They deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

We have to answer this one honestly and crookedly both, because what we can show you depends entirely on whose failure you mean. If you mean a hand that failed - a bishop discovered, after years of ministry, to have been a traditor all along - we can tell you plainly what happens. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. If the hand that gave the washing was not clean, the washing gave nothing, whether anyone knew it at the time or not. So when the truth comes to light, those who received from that hand are washed again - not as judgment on them, but as the first true entry they have had. The remedy is the same washing we give anyone crossing to us from outside.

But if you mean a different kind of failure - when the community itself wronged someone, or when an ordinary member was failed by us in some smaller, daily way - we cannot tell you, because no one among us left a word on it. Not one ordinary member wrote down what it felt like to be let down, or how the body around them answered it when they were. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. The voices missing here are not a few at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

What we can show you is stranger and may not answer what you asked. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial. Then the same council took two of those condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. That is not a community answering an ordinary member's hurt. That is a council suspending its own absolute rule for two men it had just cursed in the harshest words it owned. We never explained the difference, and no rule of ours survives that tells you when the line held and when it did not.

No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

What ended in 439 was not the quarrel itself but one specific thing: the Roman imperial state as the Catholic-aligned power that adjudicated and coerced. It persisted under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for roughly a further century and a half. It falls silent only after Gregory the Great's correspondence in the 590s.

No continuous line to any present-day communion is documented at any point. This is not a living tradition today: no church now living holds a documented line back to it.

Before anything else, understand what the thing at the center was. Not a book you could carry in your pocket. A codex. Heavy, specific, material - heavy enough that a magistrate could demand a bishop haul it out of a building and hand it over, and some bishops did. The whole of us exists because of that weight in a man's arms, and whether he carried it to the magistrate or refused.

Now the step itself. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down.

Before we answer that, we need to correct where you have put the claim. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We cannot tell you. That is not modesty - it is the shape of what was lost. A man's own fear, his wavering, the nights his mind would not go quiet - none of that is in our own words anywhere. What survives of our inner life was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights. The feelings that do survive - vindication, the burning eagerness to be proven right - survive because they sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered. Doubt does not appear there, because those texts hold up what a formed life looks like at its completion, not what it feels like in the middle when you are not sure.

What we can show you is not a practice for the unsettled mind. It is how we handled an unsettled question. At Cirta, before the whole quarrel hardened, our own bishops were asked straight out whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. That is not an answer to give a troubled soul. It is an admission that the men who would make a bishop's own purity the test of whether a sacrament is real at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

And we will show you the other half too, because it is also true. If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there. We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we gathered at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

And we can tell you the one threshold everyone crossing to us walked through. You came from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you had not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it.

Two words, cut in stone, and almost nothing else. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone carved Deo laudes - praise to God - the cry that named who we were. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in. And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

What belonging to us cost we can put numbers on, in part, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver, and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

I do not know. Not one line survives from our own communion about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole, and I would rather show it to you than paper it over.

What I can tell you instead is the shape of what we did mark, and marked publicly. Where our rival has a bishop, so do we. Two men claim one office over one city. It is a whole church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great Conference at Carthage, 279 of our bishops sat facing 286 of theirs. Our senior bishop sits at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claims the same see for its own man at the same time. So there are two primates in one city, as there are two bishops in every town. That parallel is what we built and marked and fought to hold.

And the one threshold we marked bodily, that everyone in the street could see: the washing. Where our rival says 'Deo gratias' -- thanks to God -- we say 'Deo laudes'. Praise to God. It is not just a phrase in worship. It names who you are when you say it. It is cut in stone at Bagai and elsewhere, in our own words, with no enemy holding the pen.

Marriage as a rite we can describe to you, we cannot. The thresholds we actually marked were these: which bishop, which basilica, which words at the font.

There was one place where the thing we insisted on most fiercely did not, in practice, hold - and we never hid it, but we never settled it either. We said absolutely that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cannot even find burial - and afterward took two of the condemned bishops back into full office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. The harshest words we owned, and the plainest exception to the rule those words defend, sit inside the same council's own year. We do not call ourselves inconsistent for it. We do not call it resolved either. We held both - the absolute rule and the named exception - in the same breath, and did not experience that as something that needed closing.

Whether that unsettled any ordinary member of ours, we cannot tell you. Not one of them left a word about what troubled them, what they doubted, or whether this particular strain weighed on them at all. The councils named it plainly. The households kept no record we can reach.
